text.p: Israelis lit memorial candles, wept and wondered if any lesson had been learned as they marked the first anniversary of the assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin by a right-wing, religious Jew.

While the flames flickered in Rabin Square in Tel Aviv, Israeli and Palestinian negotiators tried again in Jerusalem late on Thursday to clinch an elusive deal on a long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron.

"It is clear Chairman Arafat would like to reach an agreement -- that's what he said to me," U.S. mediator Dennis Ross told Reuters. Israeli officials had accused Palestinian President Yasser Arafat of foot-dragging.
Political divisions in Israel ran as deep as they did a year ago when law student Yigal Amir, trying to stop Rabin's peace drive with the Palestinians, shot him dead at a peace rally.

Thousands of tearful Israeli youths gathered for a night-time vigil at the site of the assassination, now named Rabin Square, opposite Tel Aviv city hall. They sang "The Song of Peace", just as Rabin had minutes before he died.
Schools across Israel set up "memorial rooms" filled with photos of Rabin and handwritten homages to the slain leader.
But at a religious high school where several girls set up a Yigal Amir fan club several months ago, one student lashed out at left-wing youngsters who held a protest outside.
"I am not saying the murder of Rabin was a good thing but why all the fuss?" she told reporters.

Right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, accused by Rabin's widow Leah of having fostered as opposition leader an atmosphere of hate that led to the November 4 killing, said more political violence was possible.
"We know there are groups -- albeit in the minority and small, but violent and radical -- still among us," Netanyahu told a memorial session of parliament.
"The murder of Yitzhak Rabin must remind us of a basic truth: peace begins at home," he said. "The choice before us today is to seal the rift and unite or widen the division and disintegrate."

The Netanyahu government opposes the land-for-peace policy pursued by Rabin and is currently locked in talks with the PLO on carrying out the partial troop pullout from Hebron, home to 400 Jewish settlers and 100,000 Palestinians.
"Progress has been made but there are still some differences that both sides are trying to overcome," Ross said as negotiators met in a Jerusalem hotel.
"The closer you get, some problems come up that are not anticipated but it's part of the overall process. I feel there is a genuine effort to reach agreement and I am hopeful."
PLO officials said Palestinian negotiators submitted on Wednesday a paper listing all the points of agreement and contention between the two sides.

They said the main sticking point was Israel's insistence on "hot pursuit" of Arab guerrillas into what would be Palestinian-controlled areas of Hebron and its objection, on security grounds, to the reopening of a road in the town centre.
Israel handed over other West Bank towns to Palestinian rule under a 1995 peace deal. But it delayed the Hebron pullback after suicide bombings in February and March.

At a memorial ceremony in Tel Aviv, Yuval Rabin, son of the late prime minister, said an incident in Hebron on Tuesday in which a religious Jew threw hot tea in the face of dovish legislator Yael Dayan, was a warning sign.
"Cups of scalding tea will again turn into hot lead for bullets and the blood of the next political assassination will pour over all of us," he said. "The writing is on the wall again."
Family and Israeli leaders across the political spectrum attended a state memorial at the gravesite on Jerusalem's Mount Herzl. A small crowd gathered as night fell to pay its respects.
"I am sorry that we are standing at the same place and it does not appear that anything (in Israel) has changed," said Yaakov Rotblit, who wrote the lyrics to "The Song of Peace".
